summaries.example: Imagine a team building a treehouse. You can talk about the wood, the ladder, and the roof separately, but the treehouse works as one connected thing. Bradley thought reality was even more tightly connected: separate parts make the best sense when we understand how they belong to a larger whole.
summaries.summary: F. H. Bradley was an important British philosopher of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. He is best known for metaphysics, the study of reality. Bradley believed that reality is a single, all-inclusive whole made of experience—feeling, thought, and choice. He argued that our usual picture of separate objects can become contradictory when examined closely. For him, relations between things are not extra links added to already independent things; both the things and their relations make sense within a whole. Bradley also wrote about ethics and argued that morality aims at self-realization, or becoming the best kind of person. He criticized the idea that morality is simply about collecting pleasure, while keeping the insight that happiness matters. In logic, he studied judgment, inference, meaning, reference, and truth. He thought ordinary statements are useful but never perfectly faithful to the complete reality they describe. His reputation later declined, partly because critics presented his idealism in oversimplified ways, but interest in his work returned. The entry presents Bradley as a difficult, original thinker whose ideas helped shape later discussions of ethics, logic, truth, and metaphysics.
key_ideas: Bradley was a leading British Idealist who was influenced by several European philosophers, especially Kant and Hegel, but he did not simply copy either one.
He argued that ordinary ideas can cause problems when we push them to their logical conclusions.
He believed reality is one whole made of experience, although everyday life shows us many people, things, and events.
Bradley thought morality involves becoming a better self through relationships and responsibilities, but he also said ordinary morality cannot completely reach its ideal.
His work on logic questioned whether ideas can be treated as separate pieces that are simply joined together.
His unusual views influenced later thinkers, including Bertrand Russell, even when those thinkers disagreed with him.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bradley shows why philosophers ask whether everyday ways of speaking give us the whole truth. His work also teaches that a thinker can influence people who reject the thinker’s main theory. Studying him helps us notice hidden assumptions about separate objects, personal identity, happiness, and truth. It encourages careful thinking about how parts depend on the larger situations in which they appear.

important_terms.definition: The view that reality is ultimately one connected whole, not a collection of completely independent things.
The view that reality is made from experience, such as feeling, thinking, and choosing, rather than from matter alone.
A careful study of what is real and how the most basic parts of reality fit together.
A way of thinking that checks whether ideas fit together without contradictions.

questions_to_think_about: Can a thing be fully understood if we ignore everything connected to it?
Is being happy by itself enough to make an action morally good?
When we describe one part of a situation, what might we leave out?
Could two people disagree about an idea because each is seeing only part of a larger whole?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “A school is just a building, teachers, students, and rules added together.” Bradley would ask whether these items can really be understood as independent pieces. A school’s identity depends on the relationships among them and on the larger activity they form. He would not necessarily deny that classrooms and students exist; rather, he would question whether they are fully independent realities.
summaries.summary: Francis Herbert Bradley was the most prominent and philosophically influential British Idealist of his generation. His project was not a straightforward adoption of Hegelianism: he drew on a range of sources while opposing dogmatic, one-sided accounts of mind and reality. His central metaphysical claim is that reality is one all-inclusive experience, often called the Absolute. This is not the private experience of one individual and is not ordinary psychological solipsism. Bradley’s argument begins negatively. He maintains that concepts used in everyday life and philosophy—such as substance, quality, relation, cause, space, time, and self—become contradictory when their implications are fully examined. His discussion of relations is especially important. A term seems to depend on a relation, while the relation depends on its terms; treating either as an independent item can produce regress problems. Bradley therefore treats terms and relations as aspects of a whole, rather than as separately existing substances. This position has often been read as a doctrine that all relations are internal, but the entry argues that such a reading oversimplifies his considered view. In ethics, Bradley argues that the moral goal is self-realization. He criticizes hedonistic utilitarianism because pleasure cannot be identified independently of the moral activity that produces a flourishing life. He also criticizes an isolated conception of duty. His social account of the self is powerful but not final, since actual social roles can be morally defective. In logic, Bradley rejects the idea that judgments are assembled from independent ideas. key_ideas: Bradley’s British Idealism was an original engagement with Kant, Hegel, and other thinkers, not a simple choice of Hegel over British empiricism.
In Appearance and Reality, he argues that familiar concepts such as substance, relation, space, time, motion, and the self generate contradictions when treated as fully independent or complete.

His criticism of relations is often misunderstood. He does not simply say that relational statements such as “7 is greater than 3” are ordinary falsehoods; he argues that terms and relations are intelligible only within a whole.

Bradley’s ethics develops through criticism of rival theories. Hedonistic utilitarianism isolates pleasure, while a strict duty theory can isolate duty; each preserves an important insight but is incomplete.
The social account in “My Station and Its Duties” is important but is not Bradley’s final position. He recognizes that an existing society may be unjust and may need reform according to an ideal.

His logic rejects the picture of judgments as combinations of independent ideas. It also investigates reference, universal statements, fictional entities, inference, and the limits of correspondence accounts of truth.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bradley’s philosophy matters because it tests the assumption that the world is made of independent objects with relations added afterward. That challenge connects metaphysics to logic: if judgments separate what is united in reality, then even accurate statements may be partial. His ethics similarly connects individual character with social practices while leaving room to criticize imperfect institutions. His influence on Russell and later debates about truth, relations, and analysis shows that philosophical influence can persist through disagreement, not only agreement.

important_terms.definition: Bradley’s view that reality is ultimately a single whole rather than a set of independently existing substances.
The position that reality consists fundamentally of experience, including feeling, thought, and will; Bradley’s version was objective, not a claim that only one person’s mind exists.
The study of ultimate reality, including what exists and how its basic features are related.
A relation of dependence in which each side helps make sense of the other, rather than one side being fully independent.
The act of referring an ideal content to reality; for Bradley, judgment is not merely the joining of separate mental ideas.
A theory holding that truth is identical with knowledge and reality, rather than merely copying an external fact.
The view that truth and reality can occur by degrees, because ordinary claims capture only partial aspects of the whole.
The moral aim of developing oneself as a complete person, understood through social life and responsibility.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining a thing by listing its properties explain how those properties form one thing?
If a society shapes our identities, how can we criticize that society when its roles are unjust?
Can a statement be useful and more true than another without being perfectly true?
Does Bradley’s holistic account genuinely solve the problem of relations, or does it relocate the problem to the whole?
What is gained and lost when philosophy challenges common sense?

summaries.example: Consider a soccer team. A player can be described alone, but the meaning of the player’s position depends partly on teammates, rules, and the game. Bradley’s idea is stronger than saying that connections are useful: he questions whether things could be fully what they are if they were completely separate. He would say the team is not just players plus links; the organized whole helps explain the parts.
summaries.summary: F. H. Bradley was a major British Idealist whose work covered history, ethics, logic, and metaphysics. British Idealism was a movement that reconsidered earlier British philosophy while responding to Kant, Hegel, and other European thinkers. Bradley’s most famous claim is that reality is a single connected whole. He joined this monism to idealism, the view that experience is fundamental. Bradley did not mean that reality is only one person’s private thoughts. Instead, he described an all-inclusive experience that contains the differences found in ordinary life. His case begins with criticism. He thought concepts such as separate objects, substances, causes, space, time, and relations produce contradictions if we assume they are completely independent. His view of relations has often caused disagreement. He argued that a relation needs its terms, while the terms are partly understood through their relations. Treating either side as fully independent leads to difficulties, so Bradley placed both within a larger whole. In ethics, he asked why anyone should be moral. He answered that morality aims at self-realization, but he developed this answer by testing other theories. He rejected the idea that morality is simply the search for pleasure, yet he retained happiness as an important moral concern. He also explored the idea that people find moral identity through social roles, while acknowledging that real societies can be imperfect and may need reform. In logic, Bradley challenged the picture of thought as separate ideas joined together. He studied how judgments refer to reality, how universal statements work, and why ordinary truth may be partial. His influence later appeared in the work of philosophers who often opposed his idealism.
key_ideas: Bradley helped renew British philosophy by engaging with continental thinkers while also criticizing them.
He believed that many common ideas look clear at first but become contradictory when we examine how they fit together.
His metaphysics combines monism with idealism: reality is one, and its basic material is experience.
Bradley’s theory of morality moves through criticisms of pleasure-based ethics, strict duty, and a social account of moral roles.
He argued that our judgments and descriptions are always incomplete because they separate things that are connected in reality.
Although his reputation fell after his death, later scholars reconsidered his work and corrected some hostile summaries of it.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bradley matters because he asks students to look beneath familiar assumptions. Are objects really independent? Is a person understandable apart from a community? Does a true sentence show reality exactly, or only from one limited angle? His answers are controversial, but the questions connect everyday experiences—friendships, responsibilities, teams, and disagreements—to deep philosophical problems about reality, truth, and morality.

important_terms.definition: The belief that reality is basically one connected whole rather than many totally independent things.
The belief that experience—thinking, feeling, and choosing—is fundamental to reality.
The study of what is ultimately real and how reality is organized.
The connections between things, such as being taller than, beside, or related to something else.
The process of drawing out the consequences of an idea, often to reveal a problem or a better understanding.
The moral goal of developing a complete and worthwhile self through action and social life.
The view that morality aims mainly at producing the greatest amount of pleasure or happiness.

questions_to_think_about: Is a person best understood as an independent individual, or as someone shaped by relationships?
Can pleasure be the whole purpose of morality?
If every description leaves something out, can any description still be true?
How might a society’s duties help people, and how might they need to be changed?
Why might a philosopher’s reputation change even if the philosopher’s books stay the same?
